rv.q: But it has its merits and one thing you can say about the Sater-Sheik partnership: it was never boring.
In a production by Lindsay Posner that never feels quite comfortable in its own thin, glittery skin, it’s lurid, overheated, often cringe-inducing and, eventually, just a tad wearing.
Sadly this musical is a turkey that has no hope of being pardoned at Thanksgiving.
It’s hard to work out, then, why this production is so bafflingly misjudged.
The difference is that Nero, for all its best intentions, really isn’t ready for prime time, whereas Spring Awakening even at first viewing seemed an instant classic.
For a show about one of the most colourful and storied characters in all history, it feels surprisingly flat.
Structurally unsound, the show needs significant reworking to fashion it into something more coherent.
This Southwark Playhouse premiere directed by Lindsay Posner hasn’t a clue why it exists.
Feldman’s detailed acting and the energy he brings deserve to be experienced up close.
Nero is a new musical that takes one of history’s most infamous figures and gives his story a fresh, contemporary twist.
Its biggest obstacle is discovering its own identity, as right now it veers between two completely different tones that don’t complement each other at all, instead resulting in an uneven watch.
While there are individual moments to impress in director Lindsay Posner’s production, overall Nero is a mess of a show that does not feel as if it has been gestating for 20 years.
Ultimately, Nero can’t decide whether it is a biting political satire, a psychological tragedy, a crude vaudeville comedy or a no-holds-barred rock musical.

Money has been spent and most people who love musicals will go to anything but sometimes a line should be drawn, and this musical is where to draw it – as a work in progress it did not progress for patently good reasons and should have been left where it was.
Whatever the answer may be, it surely cannot be Nero: A New Musical.
The score may lay itself open to accusations of being a bit of a jumble, but it is the saving grace.
Still, for all its barbed conviction, it remains an indifferent-feeling musical shackled to underbaked songs and a confused tone.
I wanted to love NERO but left feeling like the show is a frustrating mix of decent music, interesting ideas and choices that don't quite work, yet.

Over a tonally conflicting two hours, Nero, like the play itself, swings wildly from violent monster to lovestruck goof, moulded in the image of others, before eventually settling on a crazed and monstrous existence.

A cocktail, as those of us old enough to remember Tom Cruise's masterclass know, needs to bring together a perfect blend of different ingredients that, when mixed together with just the right balance, will produce a heady, intoxicating brew.

With an unfinished score in every style except the one that suits the narrative and its setting and a book so clunky not even Alan Smithee would agree to sign it, Nero is bound to be as popular with the public as the man it portrays.

cn.t: Critics find this long-gestating musical from the Spring Awakening team a muddled misfire, with confused tone and unclear purpose overshadowing Andrew Barth Feldman's praised central performance and occasional strong songs.
